en: Sutta Nipāta 4.5 Paramaṭṭhakasutta:
Dwelling in the view that "this is supreme,"...
Whatever further a person does in this world,
he calls everything else inferior compared to that;
therefore, he does not transcend disputes.
Whatever benefit one perceives in what is seen,
heard, in moral conduct, vows, or what is sensed,
having grasped that very thing there—
One sees everything else as inferior.
The wise say that even this very bond is a fetter, when,
depending upon it, one sees everything else as inferior.
Therefore, a bhikkhu should not rely on what is seen, heard, or sensed, nor on rules and observances;
he should not construct views regarding the world.
Whether by knowledge or by virtue,
one should not consider oneself equal,
nor should one think oneself inferior or superior.
Having abandoned self and not grasping,
he does not rely even on knowledge;
indeed, among the learned, he does not follow a faction.
He does not rely on any view whatsoever.
For him there is no aspiration here for either of the two extremes—
either for existence or for non-existence, whether in this world or in the next.
For him there are no dwellings whatsoever;
having investigated all phenomena, he has grasped what is truly determined.
Whether regarding what is seen, heard, or sensed here in this world—
Not even the slightest perception has been formed;
for that brahmin who does not grasp at views,
who in this world could form a conceptualization about him?
They do not construct [mental fabrications] nor do they hold them as foremost;
even the teachings are not clung to by them.
A brahmin is not to be led by mere virtue and observances.
One who has gone beyond does not return; such a one is called "Tādī.
This is the fifth discourse, the Paramaṭṭhaka Sutta.
